module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 830

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/830](https://www.erdosproblems.com/830)
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.sigma
open Filter Real

namespace Erdos830

open scoped Classical in
/--
Let $A(x)$ count the number of amicable pairs $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$.
-/
noncomputable abbrev A (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ((Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊ ×ˢ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊).filter fun (a, b) ↦ a ≤ b ∧ IsAmicable a b).card

/-- **Erdos Problem 830, Part 1**
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$. Are there
infinitely many amicable pairs?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.parts.i : answer(sorry) ↔ {(a, b) | IsAmicable a b}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- **Erdos Problem 830, Part 2**
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then is it true that
$$A(x) > x^{1-o(1)}?$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.parts.ii : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧ ∀ᶠ x in atTop,
    x ^ (1 - o x) < A x := by
  sorry

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then one can show that $A(x) = o(x)$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.variants.erdos : A =o[atTop] id := by
  sorry

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then one can show that
$A(x) \leq x \exp(-(\log x)^{1/3})$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.variants.pomerance : ∀ᶠ x in atTop, A x ≤ x * rexp (- Real.nthRoot 3 x.log) := by
  sorry

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then one can show that
$A(x) \leq x \exp(-(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))(\log x\log\log x)^{1/2})$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.variants.pomerance_stronger :
    ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ᶠ x in atTop, A x ≤ x * rexp (- (1/ 2 + o x) * √(x.log * x.log.log)) := by
  sorry

end Erdos830

findings.description: The factor `√(x.log * x.log.log)` agrees exactly with erdosproblems.com, but conflicts with the author-posted version of the Pomerance result to which that page attributes the bound. Pomerance's Theorem 1.1 has √(log x · log log log x), requiring one more `.log`. The Lean bound is substantially stronger: the ratio of the paper's exponent factor to the Lean exponent factor tends to zero, which I proved in Lean. Consequently this difference cannot be absorbed into the `o(1)` coefficient. This is flagged as questionable, rather than a definite Lean mistranscription, because the discrepancy is already present in the directly cited webpage.
findings.source_evidence: Carl Pomerance, 'On amicable numbers' (2015), author-posted version, Theorem 1.1 on p. 2: #𝒜(x) ≤ x/exp((1/2 + o(1))√(log x log log log x)); https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/amicablesv3.pdf. The same triple logarithm appears in the definition of L(x) and throughout the proof. In contrast, https://www.erdosproblems.com/830, read in its 2026-07-09 archived capture, displays the double-log formula used by Lean.
findings.suggested_fix: Reconcile the webpage with the underlying Pomerance reference. If this declaration is intended to state the author-posted Theorem 1.1, replace `√(x.log * x.log.log)` with `√(x.log * x.log.log.log)` and make the corresponding docstring correction. The webpage would also need correction.

reformulations.difference: Lean asks for infinitely many ordered pairs in ℕ × ℕ, without separately requiring positivity or selecting the orientation a < b.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `IsAmicable` includes a ≠ b, and its divisor-sum equations together with σ(0)=0 force both entries to be positive. The predicate is symmetric. If T is the set of positive amicable pairs with a < b, the Lean set is exactly T ∪ Prod.swap '' T. Since swapping is a bijection, this union is infinite exactly when T is infinite. Thus zero and the two orientations do not change the infinitude question.

sources_consulted: https://www.erdosproblems.com/830 — statement and remarks accessed through the archived captures listed below; current status accessed through the text-rendered page.

could_not_verify: Erdos830.erdos_830.variants.pomerance_stronger: exact agreement with the directly cited webpage was verified, but its attribution to the 2015 result could not be fully reconciled with the author-posted paper. The publisher exposed only the abstract, so I could not check whether the final published theorem differs from the author-posted version.
review.notes: All six declarations were examined. Apart from the source inconsistency flagged above, the statements match the cited page. The open questions remain recorded as open; the solved tags match the webpage's descriptions. The distinctness requirement agrees with the linked Wikipedia definition and Pomerance's explicit definition. Lean checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, equivalence.lean, and asymptotic_check.lean verified positivity, the counting-function membership condition, the ordered-pair equivalence, little-o/limit semantics, the eventual cube-root reformulation, and the separation of the two logarithmic rates. Computations gave A(0)=A(1)=A(6)=A(28)=A(220)=A(283)=0 and A(284)=A(300)=1. Direct access to Erdős Problems was challenged by Cloudflare; the latest available archive and current rendered page both report the same last-edit date, 28 September 2025.
